newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: FEATURE - SLOVENIA VOTERS SEEN ENDORSING ECONOMIC PROGRESS.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - SLOVENIA VOTERS SEEN ENDORSING ECONOMIC PROGRESS.

text.p: Slovenians, delighted by robust growth rates and falling inflation, look set to vote for a continuation of economic reforms when they go to the polls in the country's second general election on Sunday.

The economy of the former Yugoslav republic grew by a comfortable 3.5 percent last year, after contracting 9.3 percent in 1991 when Slovenia gained its independence, and inflation has been pushed to below 10 percent.

The pro-market government of Prime Minister Janez Drnovsek and his centre-left Liberal Democrats, which have ruled the country since 1992, are expected to reap most of the praise for turning Slovenia into the wealthiest of eastern Europe's reform economies.
Latest polls show Drnovsek ahead of the rightist Social Democrats by a comfortable four to eight percent margin.
"The biggest success of the current government was the return of economic growth and declining inflation," France Krizanic from the Economic Institute of the Ljubljana Law Faculty told Reuters.
PROGRESS AT A PRICE
But progress has come at a price. Slovenia has experienced a wave of labour unrest over wages and benefits this year, scaring off already-scarce foreign investors and their badly-needed cash.
Slovenia managed to attract only a paltry $176 million in foreign direct investment, or 0.9 percent of the country's gross domestic product (GDP).
"The new government will have to improve conditions for foreign investors in order to enhance economic growth," said Peter Stanovnik, head of the Institute of Economic Research.

Experts said the rigid attitude of the Slovenian authorities was the key obstacle for foreign investors, but hoped that would improve as the country moves closer to the European Union (EU) and completes its large-scale privatisation process next year.

The EU has replaced other ex-Yugoslav republics as Slovenia's major trading partner, accounting for about 70 percent of all foreign trade. The country signed an association agreement with the economic bloc in June and hopes to become a full member by 2001.
"Further strengthening the links with the EU is crucial for Slovenia's economic growth," said Neven Borak, head of the Slovenian Union of Economists.

The end of the country's second wave of mass privatisation, which should result in a whole new batch of companies being listed on the fledgling Ljubljana bourse, is expected to provide an additional lure for foreign money.

Some 769 out of about 1,500 companies have so far completed the first round of the privatisation process, based on management and employee buy-outs. The second stage focuses on the search for domestic and foreign equity partners.

Experts said the expected increase of domestic and foreign investment could push Slovenia's GDP growth rate to about four percent next year, although this year's growth is not expected to exceed three percent.
"This year's growth is down mainly because of a decrease in growth in the EU which is Slovenia's most important economic partner," Stanovnik said.
CONTROLLING PAY RISES, INFLATION, IMPERATIVE
But analysts said the government must continue to keep a tight grip on salaries and public spending to avoid endangering recent economic progress.
"Controlling salaries and public spending is an imperative for economic growth," said Stanovnik.
Average monthly gross salaries in Slovenia rose a hefty 14.3 percent over the first eight months of the year.

After a series of strikes in the public sector in the first half of the year, the government was forced to give in to pay demands of doctors, national TV and radio journalists, railway workers, teachers and air-traffic controllers, causing fears of rising inflation.

"It is important that the government continues to conduct careful social policy without any radical cuts in social benefits to avoid public unrest that inevitably lead to economic decay," said Krizanic.

Meanwhile, industrialists hope the government will devote more attention to reducing the high cost of capital -- long-term lending rates stand at about 12.6 percent currently -- and ballooning wage costs.
"The government should try to diminish interest rates and to provide cheaper loans to industry and exporters," said Samo Hribar Milic of the Slovenian Chamber of Economy. REUTER
